title: Why does putting a load balancer in front of app instances break things when a server stores LOCAL state (a session in App A's memory is invisible when the next request lands on App B): how do you fix it (externalize session/state to a shared store like Redis, or go fully stateless with JWTs), why does round-robin NOT guarantee equal WORK (a 5ms request vs a multi-second one), and why must health checks verify the instance can actually SERVE (dependency/connection-pool healthy) rather than merely be running?
shortTitle: Why does a load balancer break things when a server stores local state, why doesn't round robin guarantee equal work, and why must health checks verify the instance can actually serve?
keyPoints: Local state (in-memory sessions) breaks under a load balancer because consecutive requests scatter across instances.
Fix 1: externalize state to Redis so any instance can read/write the session.
Fix 2: go fully stateless with a signed JWT that carries the identity in every request.
Sticky sessions (pinning a user to one instance) is a weak fallback that breaks when that instance dies.
Round robin balances request COUNT, not WORK; a multi-second report and a 5ms lookup count the same.
Least-connections or least-response-time algorithms account for actual load, not just request count.
Health checks must verify the instance can SERVE (DB connection pool healthy, dependencies up), not just that the process is running.

s1_definition.oneliner: Local state breaks under a load balancer because requests scatter across instances, so externalize state to Redis or carry it in a JWT; round robin balances request count not work, so prefer least connections; and health checks must prove an instance can serve, not merely that it is alive.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Local state problem** – a session in instance A's memory is invisible when the next request lands on instance B.
- **Redis externalization** – all instances read/write sessions from a shared Redis store.
- **Stateless JWT** – a signed token carries the identity in every request; no server-side session.
- **Round robin** – distributes equal request count but not equal work; a 5ms request and a 5-second report count the same.
- **Least connections** – routes to the instance with the fewest in-flight requests, accounting for actual load.
- **Readiness health check** – verifies the DB connection pool, dependencies, and the instance's real ability to serve.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India has three identical counters and a floor manager sending customers to whichever is free. If teller A scribbles Rajesh's half-finished form on a sticky note on his own desk (local state), then Rajesh comes back and goes to teller B, teller B has never seen that note. The fix is a shared filing cabinet (Redis) or having Rajesh carry the form with him (JWT). The manager sending the same number of customers to each is unfair if some take 30 seconds and others take an hour. And checking that a teller is sitting there is not enough; you must check the computer and vault line work too.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Local State Problem
  ┌──────┐  req 1  ┌──────────┐  session in memory
  │Rajesh│ ──────► │Instance A│  (only here!)
  └──────┘         └──────────┘
  ┌──────┐  req 2  ┌──────────┐
  │Rajesh│ ──────► │Instance B│  session NOT here → logged out
  └──────┘         └──────────┘

  Fix: Externalize to Redis
  ┌──────┐  req 1  ┌──────────┐  save  ┌───────┐
  │Rajesh│ ──────► │Instance A│ ─────► │ Redis │
  └──────┘         └──────────┘        └───────┘
  ┌──────┐  req 2  ┌──────────┐  read  ┌───────┐
  │Rajesh│ ──────► │Instance B│ ─────► │ Redis │  ✓ session found
  └──────┘         └──────────┘        └───────┘

  Health Check Levels
  Liveness:  "Is the process alive?"   → restart if no
  Readiness: "Can it actually serve?"  → remove from LB if no
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Putting a load balancer in front of multiple instances exposes local state as a bug. A session in one instance's memory is invisible when the next request lands on another instance. The fix is to externalize state to Redis so any instance can read it, or go fully stateless with a JWT that carries the identity in every request. Sticky sessions are a weak fallback that breaks when the pinned instance dies.

Round robin does not guarantee equal work because it balances request count, not cost. If one instance gets multi-second reports while another gets 5ms lookups, both got equal counts but unequal load. Least-connections routes to the instance with the fewest in-flight requests, naturally handling cost variance.

Health checks must verify that an instance can serve, not merely that it is running. A naive check that returns "OK" while the DB connection pool is exhausted is worse than no check, because the load balancer keeps sending traffic to an instance that fails every request. A readiness check that tests the connection pool and dependencies is what keeps the system honest.

Remember one sentence: externalize state to Redis or carry it in a JWT so requests scatter safely, use least connections because round robin balances count not work, and make health checks prove the instance can serve by testing its connection pool and dependencies.
